title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 of the ai-adoption series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why is treating the first month as the whole change effort a mistake?
options: People need at least a full year before any new behavior becomes an automatic routine
Habit research puts the median well past a month, so the effort must continue
Training sessions usually take longer than a month to schedule
Tools are typically replaced within a month of going live
questions.explanation: Automaticity takes far longer than a launch window, and the dip after the novelty fades is exactly when reinforcement matters most.

questions.question: After a pilot produces a clear win, what is the right next move?
options: Use the credibility from the win to extend the change into the next workflow
Declare success and hand the work back to the operating team to maintain on its own
Pause the program until the next budget cycle begins
Rerun the launch campaign to rebuild the earlier enthusiasm
questions.explanation: Declaring victory early lets old habits return, so a win should fund the next round of change rather than end the effort.

questions.question: What does it mean to anchor a new way of working?
options: Announcing the change at an all-hands meeting and in a company email
Assigning a champion to answer questions from peers
Writing the new way into documented process, onboarding, and review
Setting a target for how many people use the tool
questions.explanation: Anchoring makes the new behavior the default, written into process and expectations so it survives the people who started it.

questions.question: Usage spikes during launch and falls sharply once the campaign ends. What does that indicate?
options: A novelty spike, because the usage depended on the event that started it
Compounding momentum, because usage was high at the very start of the quarter
A quality problem, because usage dropped after the launch
A licensing problem, because access was withdrawn too early
questions.explanation: Usage that collapses when the event stops was created by the event, while real momentum keeps running on its own returns.

questions.question: Which reading suggests momentum rather than a novelty spike?
options: High reach with high churn among people who tried it once
Steady reach with low churn and the same people returning
A sharp rise in sign-ups during the first week
A large number of one-time trials across many different departments
questions.explanation: Momentum shows up in depth and retention, the same people coming back, while a spike shows up in breadth and churn.

questions.question: Where is the cheapest next win when expanding adoption?
options: A large department that has shown no interest in the tool so far this year
A team made up of the most enthusiastic volunteers across the company
The existing users, through the next adjacent workflow
New hires who have never used the tool before
questions.explanation: Existing users already have access, the licensing, and the prompting skill, so the next adjacent workflow is a cheaper win than a cold audience.

questions.question: What distinguishes a champion from a power user?
options: A champion has the deeper technical command of the tool and all of its settings
A champion brings trust and influence, while a power user brings deep expertise
A champion writes policy, while a power user trains new staff
A champion is a manager, while a power user is an individual contributor
questions.explanation: A champion moves adoption through trust and example, while a power user moves it through practical command of a specific tool and workflow.

questions.question: A manager plans to appoint the three loudest volunteers as champions. What is the main problem?
options: Enthusiasm is not influence, and the network needs reach and available time
Three people is too many for a support network to coordinate well
Champions should always be chosen by seniority and tenure
Champions need a formal certification before they are allowed to help colleagues
questions.explanation: Selection works when it follows influence, representation across departments, and real bandwidth, not visible enthusiasm.

questions.question: Why should a support network keep operating after the implementation project closes?
options: To take over the vendor relationship and contract talks from the project team
To reduce the number of licenses the company needs to buy
Because value leaks after go-live, and peers tied to the work catch it
To train the next group of managers in how the tool is meant to be used
questions.explanation: A share of value is lost after implementation, so peers tied to the daily work, not the project, are what keep the new way alive.

questions.question: Why does concealing a setback damage trust more than reporting it plainly?
options: Employees already use AI, so silence reads as withholding the whole story
Employees assume the setback was larger than it really was and overreact to it
Employees conclude the program has no setbacks and set their hopes too high
Employees stop asking questions because they believe the answer is already known
questions.explanation: Employees already know what AI can do, so a hidden setback reads as a leader holding back rather than as good news. Reporting wins and losses the same way is what makes later claims believable.

questions.question: A program reports that 40 percent of onboarding entries touched an AI draft while 11 percent were completed that way end to end. What is the honest way to report it?
options: Announce the 40 percent as adoption and describe the rest as in progress
Report both figures with their sources, separating reach from depth
Report only the 11 percent because it is the defensible number
Hold all reporting until the two figures can be blended into one
questions.explanation: Reach and depth measure different things, and presenting reach as finished work is the start of exaggeration. Naming each number and where it came from lets people follow up instead of doubting the claim.

questions.question: A strong result published months ago is still posted after the tool failed to scale. What is the right response?
options: Leave the old figure up because it was accurate when it was published
Remove the old figure quietly so that nobody notices the change
Revalidate published claims on a schedule and correct them openly
Withdraw every claim the program has made and start over
questions.explanation: Stale claims, more than new ones, cause most of the damage once conditions change. A scheduled review that revalidates or corrects published numbers keeps the record accurate at low cost.

questions.question: A team member doubts the tool works and asks for evidence that it saves time. Which reaction is this?
options: Fear, which calls for reassurance that nobody in the team will lose their role
Skepticism, which calls for specific evidence of what the tool does
Fear, which calls for letting the person set the adoption pace
Skepticism, which calls for restating the rollout plan more firmly
questions.explanation: Skepticism is a rational doubt, and it answers to evidence, provided the evidence is specific and honest. Reassurance aimed at feelings does not resolve a question about whether the tool actually works.

questions.question: An employee says the tool will take their job, and the leader answers with productivity figures. Why does that response usually fail?
options: The figures are usually inaccurate and easy for anyone in the room to disprove
The employee hears the worry was not understood and goes quiet instead
The employee has not been trained to read productivity figures
The employee needs the figures in writing before accepting them
questions.explanation: Arguing against a fear signals that the concern was never taken seriously, and the silence that follows is not agreement. The worry goes underground, where it keeps eroding the program without being addressable.

questions.question: A leader has named the concern and shown which tasks change. What does handing the team control over the pace add?
options: It shifts responsibility for the results onto the team itself
It removes the need for any further communication from the leadership team
It lowers fear by letting people shape how the tool enters their work
It guarantees that adoption will finish on the planned schedule
questions.explanation: Fear spikes when change is imposed and drops when people have a say. A team that can shape how the tool arrives stops treating it as an outside threat.
